title: Gen Z turns to super earlier as retirement doubts deepen
full_text:
A growing number of Gen Z Australians are engaging with their superannuation decades before retirement, as financial pressures drive younger workers to plan earlier despite widespread uncertainty about their long-term financial future.
New research from MLC suggests almost one in three Gen Z Australians have already begun calculating how long their retirement savings will need to last, while many are estimating future living costs and planning annual superannuation withdrawals despite still being in their 20s.
The generation is also the most likely to switch super funds, salary sacrifice into super and seek financial advice, pointing to a more hands-on approach to retirement planning than previous generations.
That heightened engagement comes against a backdrop of subdued retirement confidence.
Although Gen Z has overtaken Gen Y as Australia’s most financially confident generation, with 45 per cent describing themselves as extremely or very confident in their financial knowledge, fewer than half believe they are on track to retire comfortably.
Across the broader population, only 41 per cent believe they are on track for a comfortable retirement and just 31 per cent expect to retire when they want.
Retirement has nevertheless become an increasingly important financial objective as Australians ranked having enough to retire comfortably alongside financial independence as their equal top life goal, while Gen Z placed it equal third with home ownership, behind work-life balance and financial independence.
Balancing long-term retirement goals with today’s financial realities remains the greatest challenge.
Nearly two-thirds of respondents identified cost-of-living pressures as the biggest barrier to achieving their financial aspirations, ahead of current income and debt, while women were considerably less likely than men to believe they would retire comfortably or at their preferred age.
MLC chief customer officer, Renee Howie, said the findings showed Australians were increasingly struggling to reconcile today’s financial pressures with tomorrow’s retirement needs.
“Having enough money to retire comfortably is now one of Australians’ most important life goals, yet most people don’t feel on track to achieve it. With cost-of-living pressures, interest rate rises and even uncertainty around what recent Federal Budget changes may mean for them, it’s understandable many Australians feel less in control of when and how they retire.
“What’s encouraging is that younger Australians appear to be responding with action, and engaging earlier with their finances. They’re talking openly and honestly about money, setting goals, superannuation and thinking about retirement well before previous generations did.”
Howie said younger Australians were looking well beyond simply growing their super balances by actively modelling what retirement itself might look like.
“Many younger Australians are running post-retirement calculations far earlier in life so they have a clear goal they can work towards. This is a digitally savvy generation who knows how to find information, but it’s more than just budgeting and planning, they’re taking meaningful actions with this information too.”
She said greater engagement with super, combined with small, consistent actions such as reviewing investment options, understanding available government incentives and making additional contributions, could make a significant difference to retirement outcomes over time.
“At MLC, we believe that a national dialogue around retirement readiness and confidence is sorely needed so people aren’t going it alone. But for individuals, if you’re unsure how you’re tracking, are worried about retirement or need support, speak to a financial adviser. If you don’t have one, call your super fund as most will be able to put you in touch with someone that can help.”
author: Adrian Suljanovic
heading: Superannuation and Investments
